newsitem.title: UK: Most Urals buyers to delay as Kirkuk looms-trade.
newsitem.headline: Most Urals buyers to delay as Kirkuk looms-trade.

text.p: Buyers of Russia Urals sour are expected to stay out of the market this week to await lower prices following progress in preparations for a resumption of Iraq's rival Kirkuk crude, traders said.
But commercial prudence will be underpinned by caution in the face of continuing unknowns about a timetable for the fresh Iraqi exports and Iraqi pricing formulas, they said.
"Refiners will wait and see before rushing to buy. Logically the value of Urals should drift downwards," a trader at a European major said.
"Most refiners will wait and see," said a major trader of Russian Urals.
The traders were reacting to a statement by the United Nations that officials of the world body and Iraq had finalised talks on a food distribution plan.
Baghdad has made the completion of an aid hand-out accord a condition for restarting crude exports under the second term of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.

The deal allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of crude over six months to raise cash to buy food and medicines in an exception to stringent economic sanctions imposed in retaliation for Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The aid plan will be submitted to U.N. Secretary-general Kofi Annan by next Monday, the U.N. said.
Iraq has said it expects to resume exports at around 740,000 barrels per day (bpd), up from the average of 660,000 bpd in the first 180-day period.

And most traders said they expected Iraq to be in a position to resume loadings of Kirkuk from the Turkish port of Ceyhan and Basra Light from the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr within a week of Annan approving the aid plan.
But it is as yet unclear how long the second phase of the U.N. "oil-for-food" programme" will be.

If Baghdad cannot delay the start of the second 180-day period, split up for bureaucratic purposes into two 90-day periods, it may have to hike export volume to about one million bpd to meet the cash target.
That would undermine prices throughout the energy complex. Some traders saw Urals plummeting to Dated Brent -$1.40 from current levels of around Dated -$0.70.
A fall of that magnitude would transform the current tight Mediterranean market where refineries are reluctant to lift sour at current prices.
Another unknown is whether Baghdad has actually requested the United Nations to scrap the original start date of June 8 and push it forward to this month or next.
"The aid plan being approved by Annan is a given, but is it going to be 90 days from June 7 or 90 days from next Monday? I have no idea," one trader said.
"I suspect SOMO (Iraq's State Oil State Marketing Organisation) will ask for 90 days from next Monday as that is what most lifters want. But whether they will get it I don't know."
The second phase of the programme officially started on June 8 but has been delayed by bureaucratic snags and disagreement over the terms of aid distribution and procurement.

Without an uptick in world oil prices -- which have tumbled more than six dollars a barrel since the U.N. deal got underway last December -- export volumes in the second six-month period will have to rise to meet the $2 billion revenue target.

Iraqi Oil Minister Muhammad Rasheed said last month that he expected the U.N. to approve unchanged price formulas for the second period of the deal -- adding he expected such approval to be forthcoming within a day or so of the approval of the aid distribution plan.
But some traders are stubbornly sceptical, noting pricing details must be confirmed by the United Nations.
The price for Kirkuk, which is indexed to Saudi Arab Light crude, was around Dated Brent -$2.00 a barrel for June liftings into Europe and WTI -$3.65 for June liftings into the United States.
-- William Maclean, London newsroom +44 171 542 7646
